newsitem.title: ITALY: Judges order Priebke to military hospital.
newsitem.headline: Judges order Priebke to military hospital.

text.p: A military court on Wednesday ordered convicted ex-Nazi officer Erich Priebke to leave a hillside monastery and serve his prison sentence in a Rome army hospital.

Priebke, who last month received a five-year jail sentence from a military court for his role in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, has been living in a Franciscan monastery near Rome since a court granted him house arrest last year.
The friars had stipulated that the 84-year-old should be moved to alternative accommodation once the trial ended, but they condemned Wednesday's ruling.
"Why a hospital? He is not sick, but he won't be well there. He'll be deeply depressed," Father Andrea told reporters.
Lawyers for Priebke sought to have their client moved to a private Rome residence and said they were disappointed by the military court's decision.

"This is an abnormal ruling," defence lawyer Carlo Taormina said. "We will consider, although we hope it does not happen, Italy responsible for the death of Erich Priebke in jail because of the illegitimacy of his detention."
The court said Priebke should be moved to Rome's Celio military hospital as soon as accommodation had been set up.
He will be allowed to receive one visitor each day, in addition to his laywers, to move freely around certain areas of the jail and to use the telephone occasionally, the court said.
The court has not yet ruled how much of the five-year sentence Priebke, who has been under custody since he arrived in Italy in November 1995, still needs to serve.
A decision is expected in October.
Prosecutor Antonino Intelisano said Priebke has about 1-1/2 years to serve, deducting the time already spent in custody.
But Taormina said on Wednesday that Priebke had virtually no time left in jail, since other legal deductions related to good behaviour while in custody must be considered.

Priebke and his co-defendant Karl Hass, 84, were convicted for participating in a 1944 massacre in which SS soldiers rounded up 335 men and boys and shot them in caves outside Rome in retaliation for a partisan attack on German occupying forces.
But it granted some mitigating circumstances and other concessions, reducing the life sentences that both Germans could have faced to five years for Priebke and eight months for Hass.
Hass was then set free because he had already been under house arrest during the hearings.
Priebke was extradited in 1995 from Argentina where he had lived openly for almost half a century.
